subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Sagittarius A*: Our Galaxy's Monster
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Sagittarius A*: Our Galaxy's Monster.

hook.text: At the exact center of the Milky Way sits Sagittarius A*—a black hole 4 million times the mass of the Sun.

buildup.text: It's 26,000 light-years away, hidden behind dense clouds of gas and dust. Radio waves revealed it in 1974.

discovery.text: Stars orbit Sgr A* at thousands of km/s. One star, S2, completes an orbit in just 16 years at enormous speed.

twist.text: Despite its mass, Sgr A* is quiet. It feeds very little compared to active black holes in other galaxies.

climax.text: Ghez and Genzel shared the 2020 Nobel Prize for proving Sgr A* exists. Then EHT photographed it in 2022.

punchline.text: Four million solar masses. Quiet for now. Our galaxy's sleeping giant.

quiz.question: What makes Sagittarius A* unusual compared to black holes in other galaxies?
options: It is relatively quiet, feeding very little despite its enormous mass
It is the largest black hole ever discovered
It spins faster than any other known black hole

details.summary: Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole at the Milky Way's center, containing 4 million solar masses in a region smaller than Mercury's orbit. Stars orbiting it at thousands of km/s provided the most compelling evidence for supermassive black holes, earning a Nobel Prize in 2020.
details.whyItMatters: Sgr A* is the nearest supermassive black hole and the best-studied. Tracking stellar orbits around it provided the strongest proof of supermassive black holes and tested general relativity in extreme conditions.
takeaways: 4 million solar masses at the Milky Way's center
Stellar orbits around it earned a 2020 Nobel Prize
It is the nearest supermassive black hole to Earth

faq.question: Is Sagittarius A* dangerous to Earth?
faq.answer: No. Earth is 26,000 light-years away from Sgr A*. At this distance, the black hole's gravitational influence is negligible. Sgr A* is also relatively quiet — it's not actively consuming large amounts of matter and isn't producing dangerous jets pointed our way.

faq.question: How was Sagittarius A* imaged?
faq.answer: The Event Horizon Telescope (a global network of radio telescopes acting as one Earth-sized dish) captured Sgr A*'s image in 2022. The image shows a bright ring of emission surrounding a dark central shadow. Because gas orbits Sgr A* in minutes, the image required advanced processing.
